summary: Defines an extensible format and MIME type for mail operators to report feedback about received email, as a machine-readable replacement for existing report formats. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5965 defines one format for email feedback reports. Each report includes an explanation for people, labeled fields for software, and the message or headers being reported.

questions: what is the abuse reporting format
how do email spam reports work
subtitle: A three-part email report format that people can read and software can process.

tldr.problem: Mail operators used different formats to exchange abuse and other email feedback. Each receiver needed custom software to interpret each format.
tldr.mechanism: An Abuse Reporting Format report is a multipart/report message with human-readable text, machine-readable message/feedback-report fields, and the original message or its complete headers.
tldr.outcome: The format provides registered feedback types and fields that can be extended. RFC 5965 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6650.

today: RFC 5965 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. It has been updated by RFC 6650 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Shared Report Format Helps
sections.content:
Mail operators exchange reports about abuse and other problems with received email. Without a common format, each receiver needs custom software for each sender's report. RFC 5965 defines the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF), an extensible format built on MIME multipart/report.

The document defines the report structure, not where reports should be sent, how their claims should be verified, or how senders and receivers establish trust. It is intended for operator feedback about abuse and related issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared report format lets software read feedback from different mail operators. This RFC defines the format but does not decide whether a report is trustworthy.

sections.title: What a Feedback Report Must Include
sections.content:
A report must be readable by people and software. It must include a copy of the original message, or at least its complete header block, so the receiver can examine the evidence. Its machine-readable part carries report metadata, and the format allows later extensions.

Each report concerns one email message; aggregate reports are outside the specification. The original message is the primary evidence. A receiver should rely on it before derived metadata and should not rely on the explanatory text if it conflicts with the other parts.
sections.plainLanguage: A report contains a readable explanation, machine-readable details, and evidence from one email. The original message or its complete headers are required.

sections.title: The Three-Part MIME Message
sections.content:
The outer MIME type is multipart/report with report-type set to feedback-report. It contains three required parts. Part one is a human-readable description. Part two uses message/feedback-report and contains metadata fields. Part three contains the full original message as message/rfc822 or its complete headers as text/rfc822-headers.

Senders may redact the third part for privacy or legal reasons, though the RFC recommends including the unmodified message because changes may hinder investigation. The report's Subject should match the reported message, except for a usual forwarding prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has three parts: an explanation, a form for software, and the original email or its headers. The evidence part is required even when the sender chooses to redact it.

sections.title: Fields in the Machine-Readable Part
sections.content:
The second part contains header-style fields, but they are metadata, not ordinary message headers. Receivers must not assume that their claims are accurate. Feedback-Type, User-Agent, and Version must each appear exactly once; Version is 1 in this specification.

Optional fields may identify the original envelope, sender, arrival date, reporting mail server, source IP, or incident count. Other fields may repeat, including Authentication-Results, Original-Rcpt-To, Reported-Domain, and Reported-URI. The meaning of some reported values depends on the generator's judgment.
sections.plainLanguage: The machine-readable part has three required fields and several optional fields. These fields describe the report, but they do not prove that its claims are true.

sections.title: Adding Fields and Feedback Types
sections.content:
Two IANA registries support extensions: one lists feedback types and one lists report fields. New registrations require a specification and are optional by default. A new required field needs a new version of the format; adding a field does not itself change the version number.

Implementations must ignore fields or report types they do not support. Experimental types or fields may only be used between administrative domains that have agreed to them.
sections.plainLanguage: The format can add optional fields and new report types through public registries. Software must skip extensions it does not recognize so it can still process the rest.

sections.title: Trust, Privacy, and Malformed Reports
sections.content:
The report format does not authenticate its claims. An unverified report can be inaccurate or deliberately false, so the RFC recommends checking its origin before taking automated action. Large or malformed reports can target parser weaknesses, and attachments may contain hostile data.

Reports may reveal private information, including a recipient address from a mailing list. Generators may redact information, but redaction can make reports less useful. Automatically generated reports can also be abused to flood a recipient. The User-Agent field is easy to forge and should not guide a receiver's decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: A report can be false, malformed, or contain private information. Check who sent it before acting, and handle attached data as untrusted.
